name: Bhai Mati Das
role: Companion and diwan of Guru Tegh Bahadur
summary: Bhai Mati Das (died 1675) was the diwan who travelled with Guru Tegh Bahadur and, Sikh tradition says, was executed in Delhi in November 1675 for refusing to give up his faith.
about: Bhai Mati Das was born in Karyala, in what is now Pakistan, into a Saraswat Mohyal Brahmin family of the Chhibber clan whose men had fought for Guru Hargobind. He became a trusted aide, and is called Diwan because he looked after the Guru's affairs. He travelled with Guru Tegh Bahadur to Assam and on the eastern tours, and lived at Chakk Nanaki, later Anandpur. In 1675 he set out for Delhi with the Guru and was arrested near Ropar. According to Sikh tradition he was offered wealth and position if he gave up his faith, refused, and was executed at the kotwali near the Sunehri Masjid in Chandni Chowk, reciting the Japji Sahib. Sikhs remember him in the daily Ardas.
kidSummary: Bhai Mati Das was a brave helper of Guru Tegh Bahadur. He looked after the Guru's work and travelled with him far and wide. When he was asked to give up his faith, he kindly but firmly said no. Sikhs remember his courage every day in their prayers.

story.title: A family of Sikhs
story.text: Mati Das came from Karyala in Punjab. His father and earlier family members had served Guru Hargobind, so loyalty to the Gurus ran in the family.

story.title: Helper and diwan
story.text: He became a trusted helper of Guru Tegh Bahadur, handling important work for the Guru, and went with him on long journeys, including to Assam.

story.title: Journey to Delhi
story.text: In July 1675 the Guru left Anandpur for Delhi with Mati Das and two other Sikhs. They were arrested on the way and taken to the Mughal capital.

story.title: A firm answer
story.text: Tradition says officials tried to tempt him with riches and honour if he changed his faith. Mati Das politely refused every offer.

story.title: Courage in Chandni Chowk
story.text: In Chandni Chowk he was put to death. Sikh accounts say he kept reciting the Japji Sahib and asked to face his Guru.

story.title: Never forgotten
story.text: Sikhs remember him in the daily Ardas, and a museum opposite Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib honours him and his brother.

teaches: Stand by your beliefs with courage and calm
Loyalty and service matter more than comfort
Keep calm and keep your prayer even in danger
festivals: Martyrdom remembrance of Guru Tegh Bahadur

facts.text: He was offered a nobleman's daughter in marriage and a provincial governorship if he gave up his faith. SikhNet names Qazi Abdul Wahab as the one offering rewards and says Mati Das found them small beside Guru Nanak's path.
Asked why the Guru was called Tegh Bahadur, he is said to have answered that the title was earned at fourteen by a heavy blow against imperial troops.
He was tied between two posts and sawn in two from the head downward. Sikh tradition holds that he kept reciting Japji Sahib and finished it even with his body in two halves.
Mughal records of the seventeenth century describe his death as punishment for challenging the authorities, while Sikh accounts stress that he refused to give up his faith.
Asked for a last wish before the saw was used, he asked to be placed facing his Guru, according to Sikh accounts.
SikhNet says he proposed to the Guru that Delhi and Lahore be torn down brick by brick, and the Guru answered by urging humility and acceptance of God's will.

The Bhai Mati Das Museum, in a former cinema hall opposite Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib, holds 169 works: 166 oil paintings and three posters. Many began as art for calendars that Punjab and Sind Bank commissioned from 1974.
In 1783 Baghel Singh built the first shrine at the Chandni Chowk site. An elderly Muslim woman, whose water-carrier father had cleaned the spot, helped him find the place.

Aurangzeb is said to have reasoned that if this one respected man could be made to convert, many Hindus from Kashmir, Kurukshetra, Hardwar and Benares would follow, which is why the court pressed so hard.

Wikipedia dates his birth to 1641 and his death to 11 November 1675, so about 33 years old. SikhNet's family article instead says 1619 (its table says 1615) and gives 9 November 1675, so even his age is uncertain.
His family had martyrs before him. His grandfather was Lakhi Das, whose father Bhai Praga is remembered as a jathedar killed in Guru Hargobind's first battle.

SikhNet's family table makes Kesar Singh Chhibbar, who finished the verse chronicle Bansavalinama in 1769, a descendant of Dargah Mall, an uncle of Mati Das. The chronicler belonged to the same extended family.
SikhNet's family table names a third brother, Jati Das, and gives Mati Das two sons, Sahib Singh and Mukand Singh. It also calls his father Hira Mall, where Wikipedia says Hira Nand.

After the executions, Lakhi Shah Vanjara took the Guru's body away in the dark before it could be displayed. He is said to have burned his own house to cremate it, and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib now stands there.
Bhai Jaita carried the Guru's severed head all the way to Anandpur, where the nine-year-old Gobind Rai performed the cremation.
A preserved tree trunk, said to be from the tree under which the Guru was executed, and the well he used for bathing while imprisoned are kept at Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib.

Baghel Singh reached Delhi in March 1783 and reportedly built eight Sikh shrines in about eight months. In return the emperor Shah Alam II is said to have let him collect six annas in the rupee of the city's octroi duties.
The site passed back and forth between use as a mosque and as a gurdwara and ended up in court. Under British rule the Privy Council ruled for the Sikh side, and the present building dates from 1930.
The photographer Gertrude Bell recorded ceremonies at Sis Ganj in January 1903, so the site has early photographs.
His martyrdom day is a public holiday in certain parts of India, according to Wikipedia.
A list on the Panj Pyare page names Mati Das, Dayala, Jaita, Udai and Gurdita as Guru Tegh Bahadur's own five beloved ones, five trusted companions.

quiz.q: What is the title "Diwan" connected with?
quiz.why: He looked after the Guru's financial affairs.

quiz.q: Which Guru did Bhai Mati Das serve?
quiz.why: He travelled with Guru Tegh Bahadur.

quiz.q: Where is a museum in his memory?
quiz.why: It stands opposite Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk, Delhi.
Bhai Sati Das was also martyred in Delhi.
